The fact that the wound is satisfactory makes a bleed less likely and whilst total thyroidectomy can be a risk factor for hypocalcaemia, this is a little early.

question_text: A 59 year old lady is referred from the NHS breast screening program. A recent mammogram is reported as showing linear, branching microcalcification with coarse granules. Which disease process is the most likely underlying cause of these appearances?

options.C: Cribriform type ductal carcinoma in situ
options.D: Comedo type ductal carcinoma in situ

explanation: Comedo type DCIS is usually associated with microcalcifications. Cribriform lesions are usually multifocal but less likely to form microcalcifications. Lobular cancers and in situ lesions rarely form microcalcifications and are difficult to detect using mammography.

question_text: A 6 year old girl undergoes a transanal excision of a fleshy polyp 8cm from the anal verge. What type of polyp is most likely to be seen?
explanation: The child is most likely to have a juvenile polyp, these are hamartomatous lesions. Cloacogenic inflammatory polyps correspond to a rare subtype of prolapsing mucosal polyps that arise around the anal transitional zone. They can rarely mimic neoplasia. Adenomatous lesions are rarely seen in children.

question_text: A 53 year old man presents with a full thickness external rectal prolapse. Which of the following procedures would be the most suitable surgical option?
explanation: As this man is relatively young and has full thickness prolapse a rectopexy is the most appropriate procedure. It will give the lowest recurrence rates. This could be a sutured rectopexy or ventral mesh rectopexy. If the latter procedure is adopted, it is important to counsel the patient around the risks of sexual dysfunction (close to prostate).

question_text: A 22 year old lady presents with symptoms and signs of hyperthyroidism. Her diagnostic work up results in a diagnosis of Graves disease. Which of these statements best describes the pathophysiology of the condition?

options.A: Formation of IgG antibodies to the TSH receptors on the thyroid gland
options.B: Formation of IgG antibodies to the TRH receptors on the anterior pituitary
options.C: Formation of IgM antibodies to the TSH receptors on the thyroid gland
options.D: Formation of IgA antibodies to the TSH receptors on the thyroid gland
options.E: Formation of IgM antibodies to the TRH receptors on the anterior pituitary

explanation: Usually IgG antibodies are formed against the TSH receptors on the thyroid gland. Which is why the TSH level is often very low in Graves disease.

question_text: A 56 year old lady is due to undergo a left hemicolectomy for carcinoma of the splenic flexure. The surgeons decide to perform a high ligation of the inferior mesenteric vein. Into which of the following does this structure usually drain?
explanation: Beware of ureteric injury in colonic surgery. The inferior mesenteric vein drains into the splenic vein, this point of union lies close to the duodenum and this surgical maneouvre is a recognised cause of ileus.

question_text: A 59 year old man is referred with symptoms of dysphagia. On examination, he has a large goitre and on imaging there is significant retrosternal extension and features of a multinodular goitre. What is the most appropriate course of action?
explanation: Sub total thyroidectomy is no longer routinely undertaken in this group.

question_text: A 56 year old man has long standing chronic pancreatitis and develops pancreatic insufficiency. Which of the following will be absorbed normally?
explanation: Pancreatic lipase is required for digestion of fat, Proteases facilitate protein and B12 absorption. Folate digestion is independent of the pancreas.

question_text: Which of the following options in relation to the liver is true?

options.A: Ligamentum venosum is an anterior relation of the liver
options.B: The portal triad comprises the hepatic artery, hepatic vein and tributary of the bile duct
options.C: The liver is completely covered by peritoneum
options.D: There are no nerves within the porta hepatis
options.E: The caudate lobe is superior to the porta hepatis

explanation: 'VC goes with VC' The ligamentun Venosum and Caudate is on same side as Vena Cava [posterior]. Ligamentum venosum is posterior to the liver. The portal triad contains the portal vein rather than the hepatic vein. There is the 'bare area of the liver' created by a void due to the coronary ligament layers being widely separated. There are sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves in the porta hepatis.

question_text: As a busy surgical trainee on the colorectal unit you are given the unenviable task of reviewing the unit's histopathology results for colonic polyps. Which of the polyp types described below has the greatest risk of malignant transformation?
explanation: Villous adenomas carry the highest risk of malignant transformation. Hyperplastic polyps carry little in the way of increased risk. Although, patients with hamartomatous polyp syndromes may have a high risk of malignancy, the polyps themselves have little malignant potential.

question_text: A 4 year old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother. He has a swelling in his right hemiscrotum. On examination, it transilluminates brilliantly. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Undertake a Lords procedure via a scrotal approach
options.B: Ligation of the patent processus vaginalis via an inguinal approach
options.C: Undertake a Jaboulays procedure via a scrotal appraoch
options.D: Undertake a Lords procedure via an inguinal approach
options.E: Division of the patent processus vaginalis via a scrotal approach

explanation: Ligation of the patent processus vaginalis is performed via an inguinal approach. There is no indication for scrotal surgery for hydrocele in young children.

question_text: A 42 year old lady presents with right upper quadrant pain and a sensation of abdominal fullness. An ultrasound scan demonstrates a 6.5 cm hyperechoic lesion in the right lobe of the liver. Serum AFP is normal. What is the most likely underlying lesion?
explanation: Linked to use of oral contraceptive pill Lesions are usually solitary They are usually sharply demarcated from normal liver although they usually lack a fibrous capsule On ultrasound the appearances are of mixed echoity and heterogeneous texture. On CT most lesions are hypodense when imaged prior to administration of IV contrast agents In patients with haemorrhage or symptoms removal of the adenoma may be required Mesenchymal hamartomas — Congential and benign, usually present in infants. May compress normal liver Liver abscess Biliary sepsis is a major predisposing factor

question_text: A 63 year old Japanese man presents with epigastric discomfort and iron deficiency anaemia. He undergoes an upper GI endoscopy, where the following appearances are found:
explanation: During upper GI endoscopy, a linitis plastica lesion may prevent gastric distension. Linitis plastica produces a diffuse infiltrating lesion, the stomach is fibrotic and rigid and will not typically distend. This may be described as a 'leather bottle stomach'. Diagnosis is made with a combination of pathology examination with endoscopy, radiological or surgical assessment. Pathologically signet-ring cell proliferation occurs.

question_text: A 21 year old female notices a bloody discharge from the nipple. She is otherwise well. On examination, there are no discrete lesions to feel and mammography shows dense breast tissue but no mass lesion. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Intraductal papillomata are the commonest cause of blood stained nipple discharge in younger women. There is seldom any palpable mass. An ultrasound is required and possibly a galactogram.

question_text: A 52 year old woman with known Hashimotos thyroiditis presents with a neck swelling. She describes it as rapidly increasing in size over 3 months and she complains of dysphagia to solids. On examination, there is an asymmetrical swelling of the thyroid gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Thyroid lymphoma (Non Hodgkin's B cell lymphoma) is rare. It should be considered in patients with a background of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and a rapid growth in size of the thyroid gland. Diagnosis can be made with core needle biopsy; however an incisional biopsy may be needed. Radiotherapy is the main treatment option.

question_text: A 34 year old lady presents to her general practitioner with peri anal discomfort. The general practitioner diagnoses pruritus ani, which of the following is least associated with the condition?
explanation: Causes: Systemic (DM, Hyperbilirubinaemia, aplastic anaemia) Mechanical (diarrhoea, constipation, anal fissure) Infections (STDs) Dermatological Drugs (quinidine, colchicine) Topical agents

question_text: A 78 year old lady presents to the surgical clinic with symptoms of both dysphagia and dyspnoea. On examination, there is a large mass in the neck that moves on swallowing. CT scanning of the neck shows a locally infiltrative lesion arising from the thyroid and invading the strap muscles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Histologically tumour has papillary projections and pale empty nuclei Seldom encapsulated Lymph node metastasis predominate Haematogenous metastasis rare Account for 60% of thyroid cancers Follicular carcinoma May appear macroscopically encapsulated, microscopically capsular invasion is seen. Without this finding the lesion is a follicular adenoma. Vascular invasion predominates

question_text: The cell of origin in virtually all pancreatic carcinomas is which of the following?
explanation: Over 90% of pancreatic carcinomas are adenocarcinomas and are thus of ductular epithelial origin.

question_text: A 3 year old boy is referred to the clinic with a scrotal swelling. On examination, the mass does not transilluminate and it is impossible to palpate normal cord above it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is likely to be an indirect hernia. In children these arise from persistent processus vaginalis and require herniotomy.

question_text: A 62 year old man presents with dysphagia and on investigation is found to have a stenosing tumour of the mid oesophagus with a single metastasis in the right lobe of the liver (segment VI). What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Radical radiotherapy to the oesophagus and liver resection
options.B: Insertion of self expanding metallic stent
options.C: Liver resection and subsequent oesophageal resection
options.D: Oesophageal resection and subsequent liver resection
options.E: Combined oesophageal and liver resection if cardiopulmonary exercise testing shows the patient is fit enough

explanation: Distant disease in patients with oesophageal cancer is a contra indication to a resectional strategy and downstaging with chemotherapy is not routinely undertaken in this age group as the results are poor. An expanding stent will provide rapid and durable palliation.

question_text: A 55 year old man presents with tenesmus and rectal bleeding. On examination he has a large bulky rectal cancer at 5cm from the anal verge with tethering to the prostate gland. Imaging shows no distant disease. What is the most appropriate initial treatment modality?

options.A: Abdomino-perineral resection of the colon and rectum
options.C: Abdomino-perineal excision of the colon and rectum with prostatectomy

explanation: Rectal cancers with threatened resection margins are managed with radiotherapy and chemotherapy initially. This is not the case with colonic cancers which are usually primarily resected. T4 rectal cancers are managed with long course chemoradiotherapy. A dramatic response is not uncommon. To embark on attempted resection at this stage is to court failure.

question_text: A 35 year old woman has undergone a wide local excision. The histology shows an invasive lobular carcinoma present at 3 of the resection margins. Cavity shavings taken at the original operation are also involved. Sentinel node biopsy was negative. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.D: Arrange for radical radiotherapy to the breast and axilla
options.E: Arrange for completion mastectomy and axillary node clearance

explanation: This patient has an extensive disease process and lobular cancers are notorious for being multifocal. In this case a mastectomy is the safest next step. Radiotherapy is not appropriate in this setting as the margins are not clear.

question_text:
A 56-year-old female is admitted to ITU with a severe pancreatitis. Thyroid function tests show:

TFTs: TSH 0.8 mU/L (low-normal), Free T4 8 pmol/L (low), Free T3 2.5 nmol/L (low).
explanation: This patient has sick euthyroid syndrome as all thyroid parameters are reduced. Graves disease and levothyroxine will cause hyperthyroidism (low TSH and elevated thyroxine/T3). Hashimotos thyroiditis is associated with hypothyroidism (high TSH and low thyroxine/T3).

question_text: An 83 year old lady is admitted from a nursing home with infected lower leg ulcers. She underwent an attempted long superficial femoral artery sub initimal angioplasty 2 weeks previously. This demonstrated poor runoff below the knee. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Below knee amputation with Burgess flap
options.B: Below knee amputation with skew flaps

explanation: The best option here is to opt for early amputation or simply palliate the patient. Above knee surgery would be needed, attempts to offer a below knee amputation would probably fail.

question_text: A 33 year old lady presented with jaundice secondary to common bile duct stones. A cholecystectomy and common bile duct exploration is performed and the bile duct closed over a T tube. Six weeks post operatively a T tube cholangiogram is performed and shows no residual stones. The T tube is removed and five hours after removal a small amount of bile is noted to be draining from the T tube site. What is the best course of action?

options.D: Return to theatre for CBD exploration

explanation: When the bile duct is closed over a T Tube the latex in the T tube encourages tract fibrosis. This actually encourages a fistula to develop. The result is that when the tube is removed any bile which leaks will usually drain through the tract. Provided that there are no residual stones in the duct the fistula will slowly close. Persistent high volume drainage may be managed with ERCP and sphincterotomy.

question_text: Where are sarcomas most likely to be found?
explanation: 40% of sarcomas are found in the extremities.

question_text: A 62 year old man presents with dyspepsia and a tumour of the gastric cardia is diagnosed. He has no evidence of metastatic disease. What is the most appropriate treatment option?

options.A: Sub total gastrectomy and Roux en Y reconstruction
options.B: Total gastrectomy and Roux en Y reconstruction
options.C: Total gastrectomy and loop jejunostomy reconstruction
options.D: Proximal gastrectomy and gastric pull up

explanation: This will require a total gastrectomy. Retention of a gastric remnant is unlikely to achieve acceptable resection margins. Resection of the proximal stomach with pull up of the stomach is not standard oncological practice for gastric cancer.

question_text: A 34 year old lady is undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholecystitis. She has been unwell for the past 10 days. On attempting to dissect the gallbladder (which is distended), all that can be seen are the gallbladder fundus and dense adhesions make it difficult to dissect Calots triangle. What is the best course of action?

options.B: Dissect the adhesions off Calots triangle and continue with the cholecystectomy
options.C: Dissect out the bile duct and perform a cholangiogram

explanation: Do not confuse cholecystostomy with cholecystectomy its a very common error and people lose easy marks as a result. Note the correct answer is cholecystostomy. The timeframe of 10 days makes attempts at proceeding with surgery hazardous even in experienced hands. However, the patient is unwell and this will not settle without some form of intervention. If only the fundus can be seen, then it may be difficult to even proceed with a sub total cholecystectomy. Therefore, a cholecystostomy can be performed and this will usually allow the situation to settle. Definitive surgery can then be undertaken in more favourable circumstances.

question_text: What is the approximate volume of pancreatic secretions in a 24 hour period?
explanation: Typically the pancreas secretes between 1000 and 1500ml per day.

question_text: A 74 year old gentleman presents with an obstructing carcinoma of the splenic flexure. Attempts at placement of a colonic stent have failed. Which of the operative options listed below offers the best solution to this problem?
explanation: Standard right hemicolectomy involves colonic division to the right of the middle colic vessels Extended right hemicolectomy involves division of the middle colic vessels and usually resection of the splenic flexure as well. The question always causes confusion and to understand it the information needs to be carefully read. Firstly, the tumour is definitely at the splenic flexure and the second point is that the operation is definitely an extended right hemicolectomy. A left hemicolectomy or even the older operation of a transverse colectomy could be considered if the patient was not obstructed. However, when obstruction is present, an extended right hemicolectomy (which involves an ileocolic anastomosis) is relatively safe even in the obstructed setting.

question_text: A parent brings her 4 year old child to the surgical clinic. She has noticed an intermittent swelling in the right scrotum that is worse in the evening. On examination he has a soft fluctuant swelling in the right scrotum that cannot be separated from the testis. It transilluminates when a pen torch is held against it. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Ligation of patent processus vaginalis via inguinal approach
options.B: Ligation of patent processus vaginalis via a scrotal approach

explanation: In children, a hydrocele is most commonly due to a persistent processus vaginalis. The swelling is intermittent and in most cases that are diagnosed in infancy the hydrocele resolves. Cases that persist beyond two years of age are best managed surgically and the surgical approach is usually made via the inguinal canal where the patent processus is identified and ligated.

question_text: Stimulation of the parasympathetic nerve supply to the bladder is most likely to result in which of the following actions?

options.A: Contraction of the internal urethral sphincter
options.B: Relaxation of the external urethral sphincter
options.C: Contraction of the external urethral sphincter

explanation: The internal sphincter is formed by the circular arrangement of smooth muscle of the bladder wall at the neck of the bladder. The detrusor muscle and internal sphincter are under autonomic control. Parasympathetic fibres cause contraction of the detrusor muscle and relaxation of the internal sphincter. Sympathetic fibres cause relaxation of the detrusor muscle and contraction of the internal sphincter. The external sphincter is under voluntary control.

question_text: A 30 year old male presents with gynaecomastia. Clinically, he is noted to have a nodule in the left testis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Leydig cell tumours are rare testicular sex cord stromal tumours (which also include sertoli cell tumours) which are associated with hormonal activity. Patients with Leydig cell tumours may present with gynaecomastia before they notice testicular enlargement. Majority are benign Histology: eosinophilic cells in columns

question_text: A 59 year old man is diagnosed as having carcinoma of the pancreas with two malignant deposits in the right lobe of the liver. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.C: Simultaneous resection of liver metastasis and en bloc segmental pancreatic resection
options.D: Pancreatic resection followed by liver resection once recovered

explanation: Pancreatic cancer has a poor prognosis and most cases have metastatic disease at presentation. There is no role in pancreatic cancer for liver resection together with pancreatic surgery as there is no survival benefit. Most centres will offer palliative chemotherapy which has improved both longevity and quality of life.

topic: Stress response: Endocrine and metabolic changes
question_text: Which of the following is not caused by cortisol in the stress response?
explanation: Growth hormone Increased secretion after surgery has a minor role Most important for preventing muscle protein breakdown and promote tissue repair by insulin growth factors Alpha Endorphin Increased Antidiuretic hormone An important vasopressor and enhances haemostasis Renin is released causing the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I

question_text: A 43 year old man has a nasogastric tube inserted. The nurse takes a small aspirate of the fluid from the stomach and tests the pH of the aspirate. What is the normal intragastric pH?
explanation: The normal intragastric pH is approximately 2 (range 1.5-3.5). Gastric acid is secreted by parietal cells via the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump). This low pH is essential for protein digestion (activating pepsinogen to pepsin), killing ingested microorganisms, and iron/calcium absorption. When confirming NG tube placement, an aspirate pH of less than 5.5 is considered confirmatory of gastric placement.

question_text: A patient is diagnosed with a Klatskin tumour which of the structures listed below is affected by this disease process?
explanation: A Klatskin tumor (or hilar cholangiocarcinoma) is a cholangiocarcinoma (cancer of the biliary tree) occurring at the confluence of the right and left hepatic bile ducts.

topic: Abberations of normal development and involution- breast
question_text: A 48 year old lady presents with discomfort in the right breast. On examination, she has a discrete, soft, fluctuant area in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. A mammogram is performed and a halo sign is seen by the radiologist. What is the most likely explanation for this process?
explanation: Lesions such as breast cysts compress the underlying fat and produce a radiolucent area (halo sign). If symptomatic, these cysts should be aspirated.

question_text: An 18 year old lady presents with extensive varicose veins of her left leg. There is associated port wine staining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A less common cause of venous insufficiency is Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber (KTW) syndrome, which involves port-wine stains, varicose veins, and bony or soft-tissue hypertrophy.

question_text:
A 46-year-old woman is referred to endocrine surgery for a possible thyroidectomy. She has a tender neck swelling. Blood results are as follows:

TFTs: TSH 0.2 mU/L (low), Free T4 32 pmol/L (high), ESR 65 mm/hr (raised), CRP 45 mg/L (raised).
explanation: This patient does not need surgery! Subacute thyroiditis is suggested by the tender goitre, hyperthyroidism and raised ESR. The globally reduced uptake on technetium thyroid scan is also typical. This should resolve without any active intervention.

topic: Stress response: Endocrine and metabolic changes
question_text: A 49 year old man undergoes a distal gastrectomy to treat peptic ulcer disease. Whilst he is recovering from surgery on the ward, which of the effects listed below is most likely to be encountered?

options.C: Relaxation of the smooth muscle of the GI tract

explanation: The stress response to surgery is multimodal and encompasses a number of physiological responses. However, cardiac output is usually increased (sympathetic nervous system induces hypertension and tachycardia). Its also results in GI tract smooth muscle relaxation. The renin angiotensin system is activated resulting in vasoconstriction and increased angiotensin II levels.

question_text: A 56 year old man is involved in a road traffic accident. He is found to have a pelvic fracture. He reports that he has some lower abdominal pain. He has peritonism in the lower abdomen. The nursing staff report that he has not passed any urine. A CT scan shows evidence of free fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A pelvic fracture and lower abdominal peritonism should raise suspicions of bladder rupture (especially as this man cannot pass urine).

question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of a Charcot foot?

options.A: Bounding foot pulses in the early phases
options.B: Often occurs in the complete absence of trauma
options.C: Erythema of the foot in the early phase

explanation: Do not confuse the early phase of Charcot foot with cellulitis Trauma (even if only minor) is a prerequisite. Patients cannot usually recall the traumatic event. The associated neuropathy means that patients continue to walk on the affected foot with subsequent deformity developing over time.

question_text: A 72 year old man presents with symptoms and signs of benign prostatic hyperplasia. Which of the following structures is most likely to be enlarged?

options.C: Right lateral lobe of the prostate
options.D: Left lateral lobe of the prostate

explanation: Carcinoma of the prostate typically occurs in the posterior lobe. The median lobe is usually enlarged in BPH. The anterior lobe has little in the way of glandular tissue and is seldom enlarged.

question_text: A 23 year old male presents with bright red rectal bleeding that occurs post defecation onto the toilet paper. He has been suffering from severe pain associated with this. On external anal examination there is a skin tag located at the 6 O'clock position. Which of the treatments listed below is most likely to be helpful?
explanation: Since the most likely diagnosis is a fissure, the correct treatment is topical nitrates. Haemorrhoidal treatments are not going to be helpful. Whilst a Lords anal dilation was the traditional treatment, there are few surgeons (and even fewer patients!) that would advocate a significant anal stretch these days as there are significant long term continence risks.

question_text: An ENT surgeon is performing a radical neck dissection. She wishes to fully expose the external carotid artery. To do so she inserts a self retaining retractor close to its origin. Which of the following structures lies posterolaterally to the external carotid at this point?
explanation: The internal carotid artery lies posterolaterally to the external carotid artery at it's origin from the common carotid. The superior thyroid, lingual and facial arteries all arise from its anterior surface.

question_text: A 32 year old lady presents with a 1.5cm pigmented lesion on her back. The surgeon is concerned that this may be a melanoma. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: 2mm punch biopsy from the centre of the lesion
options.B: 4mm punch biopsy from the centre of the lesion
options.C: Wide excision of the lesion with 3cm margins
options.E: Wide excision of the lesion with 1cm margins

explanation: Suspicious naevi should NOT be partially sampled as histological interpretation is severely compromised. Complete excision is mandatory where lesions fulfil diagnostic criteria. However, wide excision for margins may be deferred until definitive histology is available. Lesions that are suspicious for melanoma should be excised with complete margins. Radical excision is not routinely undertaken for diagnostic purposes and therefore if subsequent histopathological assessment determines that the lesion is a melanoma a re-exicision of margins may be required. Incisional punch biopsies of potential melanomas makes histological interpretation difficult and is best avoided.

question_text: Which of the following substances related to thyroid function has its effects mediated by a nuclear receptor?
explanation: T3 binds to a receptor on chromatin to induce protein synthesis.

question_text: At which of the following vertebral body levels does the common carotid artery typically bifurcate into the external and internal carotid arteries?
explanation: It terminates at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, Which is usually located at C4.

question_text: A 65 year old man is undergoing a high anterior resection of the rectum for a distally sited sigmoid cancer. As the inferior mesenteric artery is mobilised at its distal aspect some fine nerves are encountered and inadvertently damaged. What is the most likely functional sequelae?

options.A: Impaired contraction of the external urethral sphincter
options.B: Impaired contraction of the detrusor muscle
options.C: Impaired relaxation of the detrusor muscle
options.D: Impaired relaxation of the external urethral sphincter
options.E: Impaired contraction of the internal urethral sphincter

explanation: The parasympathetic nerves to the pelvic organs can be encountered in left sided distal colonic resections. If divided, there are notable effects on bladder function and this can result in impaired detrusor muscle function as parasympathetic nerves are responsible for detrusor contraction. The sympathetic nerves cause detrusor relaxation. The external sphincter is not affected. This is one of the reasons that patients may develop urinary retention following colon resections.

question_text: A 25 year old man is being catheterised, prior to a surgical procedure. As the catheter enters the prostatic urethra which of the following changes will occur?
explanation: The prostatic urethra is much wider than the membranous urethra and therefore resistance will decrease. The prostatic urethra is inclined superiorly.

question_text: Which of the following is the first vessel to branch from the external carotid artery?
explanation: Mnemonic (Order in which they branch off)Some (sup thyroid)Attendings (Ascending Pharyngeal)Like (Lingual)Freaking (Facial)Out (Occipital)Potential (Post auricular)Medical (Maxillary)Students (Sup temporal) The first branch of the external carotid artery is the superior thyroid artery. The inferior thyroid artery is derived from the thyrocervical trunk. The other branches are illustrated below.

question_text: A 6 month old boy is brought to the clinic with difficulty breathing and weight loss. On examination, he is found to have a firm para testicular mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Rhabdomyosarcomas as one of the more common malignant solid tumours in children (though all are rare). They have an aggressive behavior pattern and metastases are common. Teratomas are nearly always benign in younger children. Seminomas are very rare indeed. Malignant fibrous histiocytomas are almost never found in this location.

question_text: A 17 year old male has a suspected testicular torsion and the scrotum is to be explored surgically. The surgeon incises the skin and then the dartos muscle. What is the next tissue layer that will be encountered during the dissection?

options.A: Visceral layer of the tunica vaginalis
options.C: Parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis

explanation: The layers that will be encountered are (in order): 1. Skin 2. Dartos fascia and muscle 3. External spermatic fascia 4. Cremasteric muscle and fascia 5. Internal spermatic fascia 6. Parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis The layers of the spermatic cord and scrotum are a popular topic in the MRCS exam. A mnemonic which may help: Some Damned Examiner Called It The Testes (skin dartos external fascia cremaster internal fascia tunica Testes)

question_text: Which of the following is not an effect of cholecystokinin?

options.B: It increases the rate of gastric emptying
options.C: It relaxes the sphincter of oddi
options.E: It has a trophic effect on pancreatic acinar cells

explanation: It decreases the rate of gastric emptying.

question_text: Which of the following cell types is most likely to be identified in the wall of a fistula in ano?
explanation: A fistula is an abnormal connection between two epithelial lined surfaces, in the case of a fistula in ano it will be lined by squamous cells.

question_text: A 30 year old man is suspected of having appendicitis. At operation an inflamed Meckels diverticulum is found. Which of the following vessels is responsible for the blood supply to a Meckels diverticulum?
explanation: The vitelline arteries supply a Meckels these are usually derived from the ileal arcades.

question_text: A 45 year old woman with breast cancer is started on a chemotherapy regime containing epirubicin. What is the primary mode of action of this drug?

options.C: Monoclonal antibody to epidermal growth factor

explanation: Class — Example — Mode of action Antimetabolites — 5 FU — S Phase specific drug, mimics uracil and is incorporated into RNA Anthracyclines* — Doxorubicin — Inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis by intercalating base pairs Topoisomerase inhibitors** — Etoposide — Inhibits topoisomerase II, prevents efficient DNA coiling Platinum — Cisplatin — Crosslinks DNA, this then distorts molecule and induces apoptosis (similar to alkylating agents) Alkylating agent — Cyclophosphamide — Phosphoramide mustard forms DNA crosslinks and then cell death Taxanes — Docetaxal — Disrupts microtubule formation *=Main adverse effect cardiotoxicity **=Irinotecan is a similar drug which works by inhibition of topoisomerase I

question_text: A 6 month old child is brought to the surgical clinic because of non descended testes. What is the main structure that determines the descent path of the testicle?
explanation: The gubernaculum is a ridge of mesenchymal tissue that connects the testis to the inferior aspect of the scrotum. Early in embryonic development the gubernaculum is long and the testis are located on the posterior abdominal wall. During foetal growth the body grows relative to the gubernaculum, with resultant descent of the testis.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman sees you in breast clinic after a diagnosis of invasive breast cancer. As her sister has also been diagnosed with breast cancer, genetic testing revealed a BRCA1 mutation

Where is this mutation found?
explanation: BRCA1 is found on chromosome 17q21. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and can be passed on via both maternal and paternal routes.

question_text:
A 29-year-old woman presents with a breast abscess. She is one week post-partum and is breastfeeding.

Which of the following hormones produces contraction of the smooth muscle cells underlying the milk-producing alveolar cells?
explanation: Oxytocin is a hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary gland. The baby’s suckling stimulates the afferent nerves that connect with the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus, which in turn stimulates pulsatile release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary gland. Oxytocin binds to receptors on the breast myoepithelial cells surrounding the ducts leading to contraction of the smooth muscle and milk expulsion.

question_text:
A 64-year-old woman presents with a 5 cm mass in her left breast (32C cup). Imaging and core biopsies reveal this to be a large area of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with a negative axilla on ultrasound.

Which option would represent the most appropriate treatment plan in this patient?

options.C: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy to render the breast conservable
options.E: Wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy

explanation:
Given the size of the mass (5cm) and the size of the breast, the only appropriate option for surgical removal is mastectomy.

Breast reconstruction should be discussed with all patients who are being assessed for a mastectomy and offered in the immediate setting.

If there is a mammographic mass, palpable mass or a mastectomy is going to be carried out a sentinel lymph node biopsy should also be performed.

question_text:
A 64-year-old woman presents with a painless lump she has noticed on the front of her neck which moves on swallowing. On examination, she is noted to have a thyroid nodule and cervical lymphadenopathy. A fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the thyroid nodule reveals psammoma bodies.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid gland accounts for around two-thirds of thyroid malignancies. The tumour spreads via the lymphatics and at presentation over half of patients will have cervical lymph node involvement. Histologically psammoma bodies are typical.

question_text:
An 18-month-old child is brought to see you in clinic as his mother has noted mucus and blood staining on nappies, and has seen a bright red mass intermittently protruding from his anus. You diagnose a partial rectal prolapse.

Which one of the following statements is true regarding partial rectal prolapses?

options.A: It involves all layers of the rectal wall
options.B: It is associated with a significant increased risk of rectal carcinoma
options.C: Partial rectal prolapse is more common in adults than children
options.D: It should be treated with Delorme's procedure
options.E: The majority resolves with conservative treatment

explanation: Most cases of partial rectal prolapse in children resolve with conservative treatment.

question_text:
A 30-year-old primigravida, at week 37 of pregnancy, presents to the Parental Clinic for a routine evaluation. Her observations show a blood pressure of 130/85 mmHg, a pulse of 84 beats/min and a temperature of 37.6ºC. Urine dipstick analysis is positive for nitrates. She has a history of mild allergy to penicillin.

Which of the following medications is the most appropriate treatment of choice?
explanation: Cephalexin is the treatment of choice in pregnant females who present with urinary tract infections. It is a ß-lactam antibiotic and belongs to the class of first-generation cephalosporins. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends a dose of 500 mg twice a day for 7 days.

question_text:
A 54-year-old woman presents with a painless fixed lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast which has been present for the last four weeks. A mammogram has not revealed any abnormality but ultrasound has shown a 21 mm irregular mass.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A fixed lump and an ill-defined lesion on ultrasonography suggests malignancy. Lobular carcinoma is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario as these can be mammographically occult. Lobular carcinoma forms the second most common form of invasive breast cancer accounting for 5–15% of all invasive carcinomas. It presents in women on average older than those with ductal carcinoma, tumours at presentation tend to be larger, more invasive and have a higher percentage of positivity for oestrogen and progesterone receptors. It presents as a firm, fixed mass and can be bilateral or multilobular in 10–15% of cases at presentation. Radiographic features can include: ill-defined lesion, a mass of asymmetrical density, architectural distortions, microcalcifications or may appear benign on mammography. Lobular carcinoma usually lacks microcalcifications and this lowers the sensitivity of detecting it with a mammogram. If there is a clinical suspicion then ultrasonography should be used as well as mammography if no lesion is detected on mammography. It was found that early menarche, late menopause and age 35 years at first full-term pregnancy were more significant risk factors in the case of lobular carcinoma of the breast than other types.

question_text: What is the pathological process in benign prostate enlargement?
explanation: Hyperplasia, an increase in the number of cells, is the hallmark pathological process of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Both glandular epithelium and stromal components proliferate within the transition zone, giving rise to nodular enlargement of the gland. This hyperplastic growth encroaches on the prostatic urethra, leading to bladder outlet obstruction and the classic lower urinary tract symptoms. Although the term benign prostatic enlargement (BPE) is used clinically to describe a large prostate, the underlying histological process is hyperplasia, not hypertrophy.

question_text:
A 69-year-old man presents with a history of weight loss, altered bowel habit and feeling generally unwell. Investigations reveal a caecal carcinoma. He undergoes a right hemicolectomy. Histology reveals a large tumour that has extended into the muscularis propria but spared the lymph nodes.

What is the most likely Astler-Coller classification of Dukes’ staging for this tumour?
explanation:
According to the new Dukes’ staging it is B1 once the tumour has spread into the muscularis propria but has not penetrated through it. If it has penetrated through he propria, it is staged as B2.

The original staging system derived by Cuthbert Dukes was:

A – Invasion into but not through the bowel wall (90% 5-year survival)
B – Invasion through the bowel wall but not involving lymph nodes (70% 5-year survival)
C – Involvement of lymph nodes (30% 5-year survival).

This was revised by Astler–Coller in 1954:

A – Limited to mucosa
B1 – Into muscularis propria but not penetrating it. No nodes
B2 – Penetrating muscularis propria. No nodes
C1 – Metastasis to one to four regional lymph nodes
C2 – Metastasis to more than four lymph nodes
D – Distant metastases.

question_text:
You are trying to give the family of a young woman who has endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)-related pancreatitis, some indication of her disease severity. You decide to perform additional tests so that you can determine the modified Glasgow score (Imrie criteria).

Which one of the following thresholds scores a point in the modified Glasgow criteria (Imrie criteria) for acute pancreatitis?
explanation:
Prognosis of pancreatitis (Ranson’s criteria)

One point is given for each criterion present, severe pancreatitis = three or more points.

question_text:
A 14-year-old boy presented with sudden onset left sided scrotal pain, that started 4 h ago, following trauma to the scrotum while playing sports. The pain is severe and associated with nausea and vomiting. On examination there is an oedematous left scrotum with absent cremasteric reflex.

What is the most appropriate first line management of the above case?

options.E: Admit, watchful waiting and surgical exploration if nil improvement in 24 h

explanation:
The patient most likely presents with a case of testicular torsion.

This is defined as torsion in the spermatic cord leading to loss of blood supply to the testicular tissue. It is a urological emergency and requires immediate intervention.

It most commonly presents in children and adolescents, because in older males the tunica vaginalis is firmly attached to the posterolateral side of the testicle and therefore the spermatic cord within it, has limited mobility.

Testicular torsion presents with: sudden onset, unilateral, severe testicular pain followed by scrotal swelling. Can occur during sporting activity, trauma or spontaneously. One in three patients will also repost gastrointestinal symptoms like nausea and vomiting.

It may be difficult to perform a physical examination due to pain. If performed can reveal a swollen tender testis, which is higher than the normal testis, lying vertically and an absent cremasteric reflex (= stroking the supero-medial thigh causes contraction of the cremasteric muscle and elevation of the ipsilateral testis).

If a testicular torsion is clinically suspected, then immediate scrotal exploration within 6 h of the onset of pain is the management of choice. It is more acceptable to have a negative finding at exploration rather than delay this and result in an orchidectomy. Typically, if performed within 6 h the likelihood of saving the testicle is 90–100%, within 12 h it drops to about 20% and after 24 h this further drops to 0%.

Adequate analgaesia also forms part of the management as the pain is so severe.

Imaging is not normally performed, however the imaging modality of choice for exploring testicular swelling is ultrasound. It can be useful when a low suspicion of testicular torsion exists and other differentials are more likely.

The TWIST score system (Testicular Work-up for Ischaemia and Suspected Torsion) has been developed to determine the risk of torsion on examination findings and suggest need for ultrasonography. It consists of the following:

testis swelling (2 points)
hard testis (2 points)
absent cremasteric reflex (1 point)
nausea/vomiting (1 point)
high riding testis (1 point).

Low risk patients have a score of £ 2, Intermediate risk 2–4, High risk ³ 5. High risk patients can proceed directly to surgery; intermediate risk may require ultrasound.

Complications associated with a poorly managed testicular torsion include: infection, infertility, infarction of the testicle and loss of the testicle as well as cosmetic deformities.

Scrotal swelling: Questions that need answering when examining the patient – TEST:

T – Is it Tender?

E – Can you Exceed the lump ie get above it?

S – Is the lump Separate from the testis, ie can you identify the testis and epididymis?

T – Does it Transilluminate?

Differential diagnosis of scrotal swellings (THE THEATRES):

T – Torsion

H – Hernia

E – Epididymitis

T – Trauma

H – Hydrocoele (and varicocele)

E – oEdema

A – Appendix of the testis (Torsion)

T – Tumour/Tuberculosis

R – Recurrent leukaemia

E – Epididymal cyst

S – Syphilis

question_text:
You are checking a patient’s blood results and notice raised prostate specific antigen (PSA) levels. They do not complain of any symptoms of prostatism.

What can significantly elevate PSA levels?
explanation: Acute urinary retention can elevate PSA levels. A mildly elevated PSA level with acute urinary retention should be repeated before any further investigations or treatment, but a significantly elevated PSA level should raise concerns for advanced prostate cancer.

question_text:
A 38-year-old woman presents with a plasma TSH of 12.5 μ/L (normal 0.17–3.2 μ/L) and a low free T4.

Which one of the following clinical symptoms and signs would you expect in this patient?
explanation: A raised TSH combined with a low T3 resin uptake, and a low T4, are characteristics of hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism is associated with a dull facial expression, periorbital swelling secondary to mucopolysaccharide infiltration, decreased adrenergic drive – causing bradycardia/cold intolerance/lethargy, as well as reduced basal metabolic rate leading to decreased appetite and weight gain. Patients also experience mental slowness, depression and forgetfulness. Periorbital swelling in hypothyroidism needs to be distinguished to exophthalmos in Grave’s disease which is proptosis due to increased retro-orbital tissue.

question_text:
A 70-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with acute abdominal pain, anorexia and fever. He was diagnosed with diverticular disease of the colon six years ago and has had two episodes of diverticulitis since. There is a tender lower abdominal lump with a soft upper abdomen and sluggish bowel sounds. A CT scan shows Hinchey stage II complicated diverticulitis.

What are the most likely findings seen on the CT scan?

options.A: Colonic inflammation with an associated pericolic abscess
options.B: Colonic inflammation with a retroperitoneal or pelvic abscess
options.D: Pericolic soft tissue stranding, colonic wall thickening and/or phlegmon

explanation: Hinchey stage II complicated diverticulitis is characterised by colonic inflammation with a retroperitoneal or pelvic abscess. The Hinchey staging system is a CT-based assessment of the severity of complicated diverticulitis. Patients with complicated diverticulitis can develop abscesses, intestinal obstruction, perforation and fistula formation with surrounding organs, such as the urinary bladder, vagina or small intestine.

question_text:
A 43-year-old man has developed sclerosing cholangitis and iron deficiency anaemia secondary to chronic bloody diarrhoea. He undergoes colonoscopy as an outpatient.

A colonic biopsy would be most likely to show which one of the following?

options.A: Transmural involvement of the bowel wall by lymphoid infiltrates

explanation:
Pseudopolyps are a classic finding of ulcerative colitis. This diagnosis is suggested by presence of sclerosing cholangitis (an extra-intestinal manifestation) along with the bloody diarrhoea in the scenario above.

Ulcerative colitis affects the mucosa and submucosa of the rectum and colon, with a sharp border between normal and affected tissue. Only in severe disease is the muscularis layer involved. In early cases, the mucous membrane is erythaematous, finely granular and friable, with loss of the normal vascular pattern and often with scattered haemorrhagic areas. Large mucosal ulcers with copious purulent exudate are characteristic of severe disease. Islands of relatively normal or hyperplastic inflammatory mucosa project above areas of ulcerated mucosa (these are name pseudopolyps). Fistulas and abscesses do not occur, unlike in Crohn’s disease.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Acute Surgical Admissions Unit with a 1-day history of worsening epigastric pain, radiating through to the back, and vomiting. He is not able to find any comfortable position and analgesia is not helpful. Clinical examination reveals generalised abdominal guarding and rigidity.

What is the most definitive investigation to confirm diagnosis?

options.A: Amylase of 450 international units is suggestive of acute pancreatitis
options.B: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen
options.D: Normal serum amylase excludes acute pancreatitis

explanation: In this context, a CT scan of the abdomen is the best investigative modality in confirming acute pancreatitis. It is also useful when the diagnosis is not clear and other conditions such as perforation and peritonitis are being considered.

question_text:
You are in the general surgery clinic reviewing a 27-year-old patient referred with new unexplained rectal bleeding and you suspect colorectal carcinoma. They are subsequently referred for urgent colonoscopy.

Which one of the following statements is correct regarding colorectal carcinoma?

options.A: It is associated with a high fibre, low fat diet
options.B: It is associated primarily with Krukenberg's tumours
options.C: It is best treated by abdominal-perineal resection if the tumour is up to 15 cm from the anal canal
options.D: A Dukes C2 colorectal cancer implies nodal involvement
options.E: It is found in the rectum in 10% of cases in adults under 65 years

explanation: In 1932, the British pathologist Cuthbert Dukes (1890 – 1977) devised a classification system for colorectal cancers. An adaptation to his original classification was proposed by Americans Astler and Coller in 1954 – this further subdivided Stages B and C. Stage C2 is defined as penetrating through the muscularis propria, with lymph node involvement.

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman with type II diabetes presents to the surgical team with fever and right upper quadrant pain after having recently been treated for cholecystitis. Further investigation reveals that she has developed a liver abscess. The initial report for the blood cultures sent shows Gram-negative rods.

Which of these bacteria is most likely to be responsible?
explanation: Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli are two of the most frequently isolated pathogens in liver abscesses. They are both Gram-negative rods.

question_text:
A 67-year-old man who is an alcoholic presents to the Emergency Department with severe chest pain following prolonged episodes of vomiting. A computed tomography (CT) scan reveals oesophageal perforation with associated mediastinitis.

Which artery supplies the upper one-third of the oesophagus?
explanation: The oesophagus is divided into three concerning its blood supply. The inferior thyroid artery supplies the upper third; the middle third is supplied by direct branches from the descending thoracic aorta (oesophageal arteries); finally, the distal third is supplied by ascending branches from the left gastric artery.

question_text:
A 63-year-old woman is seen with an enlarging mass in her thyroid and difficulty swallowing. She is later diagnosed with follicular carcinoma of the thyroid.

Which one of the statements is correct regarding follicular carcinoma of the thyroid?

options.A: It can be diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
options.B: It can be monitored for recurrence by calcitonin levels
options.C: The most common presentation is a hoarse voice
options.D: It has a higher incidence in iodine-deficient regions of the world
options.E: It is most common at puberty

explanation: Follicular carcinoma occurs more commonly in the Caucasian population, with an incidence higher in areas of the world where there is a higher incidence of iodine deficiency.

question_text:
You are incising and draining a perianal abscess and the consultant asks you about the anal canal and its anatomical relations.

How would you best describe the canal?

options.A: The canal lies above the levator ani muscle
options.B: The canal has no longitudinal muscular coat
options.C: The canal has lymphatic drainage via the inguinal lymph nodes
options.D: The canal has an external sphincter innervated by sympathetic fibres from the pelvic plexus
options.E: The canal is lined by columnar epithelium below the dentate line

explanation:
Lymph from the lower anal canal drains via the superficial inguinal nodes. The levator ani forms part of the deep external anal sphincter and the canal lies below this muscle. Lymph from the lower anal canal drains via the superficial inguinal nodes. The external anal sphincter is innervated by the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), while the internal sphincter receives a sympathetic supply from the pelvic plexus. The upper anal canal is thrown into vertical folds called anal columns, seen below in the image. Above the dentate line, which is visible in the image as a wavy line at the level of the internal anal sphincter, the canal is lined by columnar epithelium; below this level, this changes to squamous epithelium.

The dentate line represents the border between the hindgut and ectoderm. Drainage above the level of the dentate line is therefore into the inferior mesenteric vein territory via the mesorectum.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman is referred to the general surgical clinic by her General Practitioner with a 2-month history of lethargy, intermittent per rectal blood loss and unintentional weight loss. She has experienced episodes of abdominal pain but is currently well and pain-free. Bloods shows microcytic anaemia and a stool sample is negative for infection. She undergoes a colonoscopy and biopsies, which are diagnostic for Crohn’s disease.

Which histological feature is most in keeping with this diagnosis?

options.D: Shallow mucosal ulceration in a confluent pattern without skip lesions

explanation: Transmural inflammatoryinfiltration on colonic biopsy is pathognomic of Crohn’s disease but is not seen in ulcerative colitis. In Crohn’s disease, there is transmural granulomatous inflammation which tends to predominantly affect the terminal ileum and proximal small bowel, but patchy inflammation can occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Although differential diagnoses for this patient could include either ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease, the presence of transmural inflammatory infiltration would be diagnostic of Crohn’s disease.

question_text:
A 68-year-old woman undergoes superficial femoral artery angioplasty after developing critical lower limb ischaemia. Two days later she complains of pain and you observe a pulsatile swelling in the left groin.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The scenario describes the case of a pseudo-aneurysm occurring secondary to the puncture of the femoral arterial wall that occurred during the procedure. This is a common side-effect of femoral punctures (can occur in up to 8% of procedures). Due to the breach in the vessel wall the blood leaks through but remains contained by the adventitia. It presents as a painful, tender, pulsatile mass with or without erythema of the overlying skin. Risk of rupture of a pseudo-aneurysm is higher due to the poor wall support and therefore requires immediate treatment when identified. Ultrasound can show turbulent flow causing the ‘yin–yang sign’ indicating bidirectional flow. Other complications associated with peripheral angioplasty include: infection, dissection of the artery, distal embolization, arterial rupture or spasm and in stent re-stenosis/thrombosis.

question_text:
You are treating a 52-year-old man with renal calculi. He has already had three admissions to the Emergency Department with renal colic.

What is most likely to predispose individuals to renal tract calculi?
explanation: Stones in the renal tract occur due to an increased concentration of urinary solutes such as calcium, uric acid and oxalic acid, or due to an increased concentration of urine during dehydration. Gout is caused by high uric acid levels and patients with gout are also at an increased risk of forming uric acid stones as uric acid deposits build in the kidney.

question_text:
A 54-year-old woman has undergone some blood tests, as part of an employment health screen. She reports she is in good health and does not have any particular symptoms. She is taking bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg for hypertension, and her BP is 132/82 mmHg. The only abnormality is a serum calcium concentration of 2.94 mmol/l (normal 2.20–2.60 mmol/l).

Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism is a common cause of hypercalcemia, especially in asymptomatic patients. It is most often caused by a single parathyroid adenoma, leading to excessive production of parathyroid hormone (PTH). This results in increased calcium resorption from bone, increased renal calcium reabsorption, and increased production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3. The patient's serum calcium concentration of 2.94 mmol/L is more consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism than with the mild hypercalcemia typically caused by thiazide diuretics.

question_text:
A 54-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with severe upper abdominal pain which is constant and localised to the right upper quadrant. She is tachycardic and pyrexial, with a positive Murphy’s sign. A diagnosis of cholecystitis is made. She is treated with antibiotics and is offered a ‘hot’ cholecystectomy.

Concerning this diagnosis and its treatment, which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: The cystic duct is a boundary of the cystohepatic triangle
options.B: Ultrasound is more sensitive than computerised tomography (CT) in the diagnosis of cholecystitis
options.C: Murphy's sign is pathognomonic for common bile duct stones
options.D: The common bile duct lies anterior to the portal vein in the free edge of the lesser omentum
options.E: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is the first-line investigation for gallstones

explanation: The boundaries of the cystohepatic triangle (Calot’s) are the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver. The triangle's contents include the right hepatic artery, cystic artery, cystic lymph node, connective tissue and lymphatics.

question_text:
You have been asked to see a 63-year-old woman in the follow-up Breast Clinic who is 2.5 years following her diagnosis of a 34 mm invasive lobular breast cancer. She is asking you questions about her diagnosis.

Which of the following is most likely to be correct regarding a diagnosis of breast cancer?

options.A: Lobular cancers tend to be more often multifocal than ductal cancers
options.B: In men there will be a familial tendency in the majority of cases
options.C: Paget's disease of the nipple is associated with a good prognosis
options.D: Inflammatory breast cancer typically presents as a discrete, well-defined mass
options.E: The most common type of invasive breast cancer is lobular carcinoma

explanation: Lobular invasive carcinoma is more often multifocal and bilateral at diagnosis than ductal invasive carcinoma.

question_text:
Inflammatory aortic aneurysms are possibly a more severe form of degenerative abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). They can be life threatening if untreated.

Which one of the following may lead you to confirm or suspect inflammatory aortic aneurysm?

options.A: They are always associated with an elevated procalcitonin level
options.B: They can present with abdominal pain
options.C: They are diagnosed exclusively by CT angiography
options.D: They do not require surgical intervention
options.E: They are more common in women than men

explanation:
Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysms are a variant of AAA, forming 5–10% of all AAA cases. They are most commonly found in younger patients (presentation age 5–10 years younger than presentation of atherosclerotic AAA), in the infrarenal abdominal aorta and are symptomatic. Symptoms include abdominal and/or back pain, fevers and weight loss. Risk factors include: male gender, smoking and family history. They are commonly associated with a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (90% of cases) and inflammatory markers. They are detected with CT scans/MRI, showing a cuff of perianeurysmal tissue and inflammatory changes. These spare the posterior wall. Radiological appearances relate to thickening of the adventitia with abundant inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells).

Initial treatment may require smoking cessation, steroids and immunosuppressive medication but definitive treatment is via surgery (open repair or EVAR). The inflammation involves the retroperitoneum as well leading to retroperitoneal fibrosis, causing entrapment of the ureters and progressively renal failure.

question_text:
A 50-year-old patient presents with renal colic, and renal calculi are seen on imaging. Testing the urine reveals it is acidic.

What type of stones are most likely to form in this patient's urine?
explanation: Cystine and urate stones form in acidic urine and urine alkalisation forms part of the treatment of these types of stones. Cystine stones are poorly radiopaque on X-ray but can usually be seen on CT.

question_text:
A 54-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of sweating, headache, constipation and itchy lesions over his back. His BOP is 162/94 mmHg and pulse 102/min. 24 h urinary catecholamines, metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid are elevated. CT and 131I-meta-iodo-benzyl-guanidine scans confirm a phaeochromocytoma. He is also has a medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia II (MEN II) is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. MEN II has three distinct subtypes – MEN IIA, MEN IIB, and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma only. MEN IIA describes the association of medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytomas and parathyroid tumours. Patients with pheochromocytomas may present with hypertension, tachycardia, sweating and headaches. Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis in patients with MEN IIA manifests as multiple pruritic scaly skin lesions in the scapular area of the back.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man patient undergoes an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for a follow up of Barrett’s oesophagus.

What is the most likely histology of Barrett’s oesophagus?
explanation: Barrett’s oesophagus occurs due to metaplasia of the cells in the lower portion of the oesophagus, from the stratified squamous epithelium to the simple columnar epithelium. It occurs due to prolonged reflux and is considered a precursor for the development of oesophageal carcinoma.

question_text:
A 63-year-old woman is seen in the General Surgery clinic after having a positive result in a faecal occult blood test. She is due to undergo colonoscopy for change in bowel habit.

Which of the following is the most common category for the development of colorectal cancers?
explanation: Around 65% of colorectal cancers are thought to be sporadic – ie the genetic mutations present within these cancers are not inherited. Important risk factors in developing sporadic colorectal cancer include age, diet rich in red meat and low in fibre, smoking and obesity. Fewer than 10% of patients have a true inherited predisposition to colorectal cancer and these cases are subdivided according to whether or not colonic polyps are a major disease manifestation.

question_text:
A 48-year-old woman is found to have high serum calcium and is subsequently diagnosed with hyperparathyroidism caused by a superior parathyroid gland adenoma. She is later booked for superior parathyroidectomy surgery.

From which pharyngeal pouch do the superior parathyroid glands develop?
explanation: The 4th pharyngeal pouch forms the superior parathyroid glands and a diverticulum called the ultimobranchial body. The cells of this body migrate into the thyroid gland, differentiating into the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland which produce calcitonin.

question_text:
A 69-year-old smoker presents with painless haematuria and weight loss. He is diagnosed with bladder cell carcinoma.

Which one of the following statements is correct with regard to this diagnosis?

options.A: The most common chromosomal abnormality is the deletion of chromosome 9
options.B: Schistosomiasis is associated with adenocarcinoma of the bladder
options.C: Transitional cell carcinoma is the least common histological type
options.D: Smoking is not a significant risk factor for bladder cancer
options.E: Painless haematuria is uncommon in bladder cancer

explanation: Deletion of chromosome 9 is the most common chromosomal abnormality, along with alterations in the tumour suppressor genes p53 and Rb.

question_text:
During an oncology department multi-disciplinary meeting the consultant oncologist mentions that a patient has a very radiosensitive tumour. The consultant, therefore, recommends radiotherapy as part of the management plan.

Which of the following tumours is this consultant most likely referring to?
explanation: Seminoma is a very radiosensitive tumour. Standard treatment for seminoma after unilateral orchidectomy is radiation therapy, usually 20-40 Gy to the para-aortic regions up to the diaphragm (a higher dose is used for patients with a nodal mass); the ipsilateral ilioinguinal region is not treated routinely. Occasionally, the mediastinum and left supraclavicular regions are also irradiated, depending on the clinical stage.

question_text:
A 55-year-old man with a family history of abdominal aortic aneurysm is asking about screening for the condition.

When and how is screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm performed?

options.A: One-off ultrasound for all men 60 years and older
options.B: One-off ultrasound for all men 65 years and older
options.C: One-off ultrasound for all men 55 years and older
options.D: One-off ultrasound for all men 70 years and older
options.E: One-off ultrasound for all men and women 65 years and older

explanation: All men at the age of 65 years are offered an ultrasound to screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm.

question_text:
You are seeing a patient in the joint oncology clinic who is about to start a course of radiotherapy for adjuvant treatment of breast cancer. While waiting for the oncologist she asks you questions regarding radiotherapy as a general principle.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding radiotherapy?

options.A: The most common early side effects of radiotherapy are lethargy and skin reactions
options.B: Brachytherapy is a slow duration method of administering radiotherapy for patients with significant, eg pulmonary, pathology and therefore need a more gentle regimen
options.C: Radiotherapy has no role in the management of breast cancer
options.D: External beam radiotherapy is only given after mastectomy
options.E: Radiotherapy should be avoided in patients over 70 years old

explanation: Cancer patients are treated by external beam interstitial or intracavity radiotherapy. The effects of radiotherapy depend upon the dose, the tumour size, the tumour proliferation rate, the tumour radiosensitivity and the presence of anaemia and vascular disease. Radiotherapy can be palliative or curative. Lethargy is the most common side-effect. Skin effects are becoming less common as the more advanced radiotherapy machines are able to deliver peak dose below the level of the skin.

question_text:
A 68-year-old woman presents with symptoms of dyspepsia. She has tested positive for Helicobacter pylori infection and been started on proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and eradication therapy.

Which one of the following tests, in common usage, has the highest combined sensitivity and specificity when used to detect Helicobacter pylori infection?

options.D: Serology for H. pylori IgG antibodies

explanation: The urea breath test detects radiolabelled carbon dioxide in the breath after ingesting radiolabelled urea (sensitivity 95%, specificity 96%).

question_text:
An 81-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a grossly distended tympanic abdomen and absolute constipation. He also appears confused. A plain abdominal X-ray reveals a grossly dilated large intestine but no evidence of pneumoperitoneum.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Computerised tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis
options.C: Rigid sigmoidoscopy and flatus tube insertion

explanation: For this scenario, the differential diagnosis is pseudo-obstruction, sigmoid volvulus and carcinoma of the distal colon/rectum. Computerised tomography of the abdomen and pelvis is the best option, as it permits the diagnosis to be obtained and the correct treatment instituted. Pseudo-obstruction may be associated with an underlying precipitating condition such as renal failure, electrolyte abnormalities, myxoedema, stroke, myocardial infarction, chest infection and retroperitoneal malignancy. Medical management comprises correction of electrolyte abnormalities, treatment of the underlying cause and use of the anticholinesterase inhibitor neostigmine (with heart monitor surveillance).

question_text:
You are discussing cases in the urology MDT. The pathologist discusses the details of some of the cancers encountered at the meeting.

Which one of the following malignancies is most commonly multi-centric?
explanation: Transitional cell carcinomas can occur anywhere in the urothelium and multi-centricity and recurrence are common.

question_text:
A 69-year-old woman presents with bright red rectal bleeding. On examination, a firm mass is palpable in the proximal rectum. A rectal biopsy confirms the presence of invasive rectal adenocarcinoma and she proceeds to abdominoperineal resection.

Which group of lymph nodes primarily drain the lower part of the anal canal?
explanation: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes run parallel to and below the inguinal ligament and vertically along the great saphenous vein. In the perineum, it drains the lower part of the anal canal and the vagina. It is also involved in the drainage of external genitalia (excluding the testes), the lower abdominal wall below the umbilicus and the lower limb. The pelvic part of the rectum and the anal canal represent different lymph drainage territories. The pectinate line separates the two territories, but communication does exist between them (i.e. the lymphatics of the anal canal communicate with the perineal and rectal lymphatics). The lymph of the perineum and the anal canal is drained to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, whereas the lymph of the pelvic territory flows to the iliac and lumbar nodes.

question_text:
You are seeing a 43-year-old patient with frank jaundice, pruritus, pale stools and dark urine. Blood tests show a pattern consistent with obstructive jaundice and an ultrasound scan shows dilated intra- and extra-hepatic ducts.

Which one of the following statements is true regarding obstructive jaundice?

options.A: Gallstones are the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice in the UK
options.B: There is an excess of urobilinogen in the urine
options.C: Pancreatic head carcinoma is the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice in the UK
options.D: Conjugated bilirubin is increased in pre-hepatic jaundice
options.E: Alkaline phosphatase is characteristically low in obstructive jaundice

explanation: Gallstones are the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice in the United Kingdom. In this patient, jaundice is caused by an obstructing stone in the common bile duct (CBD) – the pressure in the system proximal to this area leads to dilatation of intra- and extra-hepatic biliary ducts proximal to the CBD.

question_text:
During a difficult vaginal delivery, the senior house officer (SHO) on call was asked to come and make an episiotomy. She made a midline episiotomy and in doing so cut too far through the perineal body into the structure immediately posterior.

Which one of the following structures did she cut?
explanation:
An episiotomy is a perineal incision used in labour. The episiotomy has the effect of enlarging the distal birth canal – often the purpose is to prevent trauma to and damage of the perineal structures in breech or forceps delivery, in which there is a risk of this occurring.

A midline episiotomy is made from the posterior vagina through the perineal body with a risk of damage to the external anal sphincter if extended too far. The rectum can also be damaged with this procedure.

Most episiotomies are, however, posterolateral rather than midline – this procedure is safer and avoids the risk of damage to the external anal sphincter and rectum.

question_text:
You are in breast clinic reviewing a patient with a lesion detected via the national screening programme. You have read a recent article regarding the need to be conscious of bias in such screening programmes.

In general, screening programmes for cancer are susceptible to which one of the following?
explanation: Results of screening programmes for cancer are limited by selection, length and lead-time bias. Lead-time bias occurs when screening advances the date at which diagnosis is made. This, therefore, lengthens the calculated survival time without necessarily altering the date of death. Length bias can also affect screening programmes. This is the tendency for screening to detect a disproportionate number of cancers that are slow-growing and have a better prognosis anyway.

question_text:
You are reviewing a patient with a rash on their legs and a diagnosis of thrombophlebitis migrans is made. Additional investigations may be required.

With which of the following is this associated?
explanation: Thrombophlebitis migrans, also known as Trousseau’s sign of malignancy, is a migratory thrombophlebitis causing recurrent episodes of superficial thrombophlebitis in the low extremities. It has a strong association with visceral carcinoma, most commonly adenocarcinoma of the pancreas, lung, stomach and genital tract.

question_text:
A 35-year-old woman currently being treated for malignant melanoma has two first-degree relatives who have also been diagnosed (her mother and older sister). She has a young daughter and they are referred on to a genetic counselling service.

Which of the following are associated with a high risk for developing melanoma?
explanation: Familial melanoma is recognised in around 1–2% of patients when two first-degree relatives also have melanoma. Although many genetic causes are unrecognised and unstudied, many familial links have been found. BRCA1 carries with it a higher risk of melanoma, along with breast and ovarian cancer.

question_text:
A 12-year-old boy undergoes a diagnostic laparoscopy for right iliac fossa pain. The appendix looks normal but prominent lymph nodes are noted in the small bowel mesentery.

Which of the following best describes the small bowel mesentery?

options.B: Blood vessels traversing the small bowel supply the large bowel
options.C: Contains goblet cells in the epithelium of the duodenum only
options.D: Is attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the mesentery proper
options.E: Receives its blood supply from the inferior mesenteric artery

explanation: The small bowel mesentery contains the superior mesenteric artery, which supplies the mid-gut; this includes the large bowel as far as the distal transverse colon. The veins in the mesentery are all tributaries of the portal system. The root of the small bowel mesentery extends from a point to the left of the L2 vertebra, at the duodenojejunal junction, down to the right sacroiliac joint.

question_text:
You are assisting in a sentinel node biopsy for a patient with known breast cancer. You have difficulty locating the sentinel node but do so with a combination of blue dye and radioisotope.

Which of the following statements about sentinel node biopsy is correct?

options.A: Lymphoscintigraphy can be performed up to one week in advance of the procedure
options.B: Blue dye is contraindicated in pregnancy
options.C: Patent blue dye can cause anaphylaxis
options.D: Sentinel node biopsy has no role in multifocal breast cancer
options.E: The sentinel node is always located in the axilla

explanation: Currently, the use of blue dye is not recommended during sentinel node biopsy in patients who are pregnant. However, this is generally due to the risk of anaphylaxis rather than the foetal exposure to methylene blue – recent research into this topic suggests that the foetal risk is minimal.

question_text:
During a hemihepatectomy for hepatocellular carcinoma, the Consultant points to an H-shaped arrangement of structures on the visceral surface.

Which structures form this ‘H’ shape?

options.B: Gallbladder, IVC, ligamentum teres, ligamentum venosum, porta hepatis
options.C: Porta hepatis, IVC, gallbladder, falciform ligament
options.D: Ligamentum teres, IVC, gallbladder, falciform ligament
options.E: Gallbladder, portal vein, ligamentum teres, hepatic veins

explanation: These five structures form the ‘H’ shape that divides the visceral surface of the liver. The gall bladder can be seen to the right of the image, the inferior vena cava (IVC) superiorly and the ligamentum teres towards the lower left.

question_text:
You are seeing a 75-year-old man in the Emergency Department (ED) with gross abdominal distension and prominent superficial abdominal veins. He has shifting dullness and you diagnose ascites secondary to chronic liver disease.

Which one of the following statements is correct regarding ascites?

options.A: A high serum-ascites albumin gradient (> 1.1) indicates a transudate such as pancreatitis
options.B: A low serum-ascites albumin gradient (< 1.1) indicates an exudate such as hereditary angioedema
options.C: A high serum-ascites albumin gradient (> 1.1) indicates an exudate such as malignancy
options.D: Ascitic fluid analysis is not useful in determining the cause of ascites
options.E: A low serum-ascites albumin gradient (< 1.1) indicates a transudate such as cirrhosis

explanation: An exudate ascites is defined by a low serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) < 1.1. Exudative ascites are associated with malignancy, pancreatitis and hereditary angioedema.

question_text:
